description: Quantum Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Covert Quantum Computing - a new quantum security paradigm
talks.teaser: Shows how co-tenants on a shared superconducting quantum processor can sense each other's jobs through crosstalk, and how to keep a computation covert.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the expected move to multi-tenant quantum computing, where several users share one quantum processor to avoid idle hardware. It defines covert quantum computing as a guarantee that one user cannot detect whether another is running a computation. Covertness matters because a neighbor who can see activity could learn about an algorithm or its results, correlate usage spikes with insider news, or time a fault injection against someone else's job.

The speaker outlines the quantum software and control stack, then focuses on the qubits themselves. Two-qubit gates leak noise onto neighboring qubits, so a user holding nearby qubits can induce bit flips or detect activity. Prior work on this crosstalk was summarized, including attacks that corrupt a victim's circuit. The experiments used Ramsey interferometry on IQM and IBM superconducting hardware. They found the expected nearest-neighbor crosstalk, plus unexpected long-range effects several hops away, which the speaker suspects come from microwave pulses leaking onto nearby control lines.

The practical takeaway is that these experiments can be reproduced by anyone with a free quantum cloud account, and no quantum background is needed. Suggested next steps include compilers that optimize for covertness, alternative detection methods, and comparing ion-trap and neutral-atom machines. The speaker also notes that covertness applies only at the physical-qubit level, not to error-corrected logical qubits.

talks.title: Q Day - the Early Years
talks.teaser: Maps the likely opening moves of a quantum attack on public-key cryptography, from forged code signatures and root CAs to Bitcoin's exposed keys.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that the popular picture of a quantum computer suddenly breaking all encryption at midnight is wrong. The speaker expects a slow start with a few machines, most likely run by nation states rather than cloud providers, and attackers who pick targets carefully because each costly run yields only a handful of results. Forgery, not decryption, is presented as the more likely first move.

The hardware estimates are the core evidence. The speaker walks through falling qubit requirements for RSA and ECC, from earlier estimates in the tens of millions down to figures under a million, and newer architectures that trade run time against qubit count. The most probable early targets are signing keys, code-signing pipelines, root certificate authorities, secure boot chains, DNSSEC zones and e-passports, since one forged trust anchor can silently undermine everything beneath it. Bitcoin gets its own section, covering exposed public keys, mempool front-running and the proposed BIP-360 and BIP-361 changes, and the speaker doubts the network will be ready in time.

The closing advice is to expect a few years of forgery and triage before decryption becomes practical, around year three by the speaker's estimate. Organizations should start a cryptographic inventory now, using a CycloneDX bill of materials, and plan for devices that cannot be upgraded to post-quantum algorithms.
